name: Strangler Fig and Incremental Migration
intent: Replace a running system one slice at a time behind a routing layer, checking the new slice against the old one before real users see it and keeping a way back, instead of rewriting everything and switching once.
scenario: A legacy shop has 8 slices (accounts, catalog, search, cart, checkout, orders, invoices, reports) and serves 369 thousand requests a day. A big-bang rewrite takes 169 days before a single real user touches it, then switches all traffic at once: with no shadow run, hidden bugs hit 22,269 requests before they are fixed forward. A strangler migration puts a router in front, moves one slice at a time, and the first users reach the new system on day 22. With parity checks the same bugs cost 49 requests; with a ramp but no parity checks they cost 670. Cutting slices to a single endpoint each limits exposure further, but 24 slices and 12 data links across the boundary are a lot to run.
problem: A big-bang rewrite delivers nothing until the end, copies a moving target, and stakes everything on one cutover, often with no practical way back to the old system. The strangler fig pattern, named by Martin Fowler after the strangler fig, a plant that grows around a host tree and eventually replaces it, avoids that: a routing layer (a proxy, gateway or facade) sits in front of the legacy system, and one slice of functionality at a time is built in the new system and routed to it, until the old one has nothing left to serve and can be removed. Each slice is a small, reversible release. The parts that make it safe are easy to skip: running the new slice in shadow mode to compare its answers with the legacy system's before users see them (parity checks), ramping traffic in steps with a monitor that triggers rollback, and keeping the shared data consistent across the boundary while both systems are live. Done badly it becomes a migration that never finishes, with two systems to run for years. Practitioners disagree on slice size and on how much of the data to move early, and the right answer depends on how coupled the slices are.

howItWorks.title: Put a routing layer in front
howItWorks.text: All traffic first goes through a router, such as a reverse proxy, an API gateway or a facade in the application. At the start it sends everything to the legacy system, and nothing changes for users. The router is the seam where the new system will take over, one route at a time, and it is also the switch that rolls a slice back.

howItWorks.title: Choose slices by seam, not by size
howItWorks.text: Pick a slice that has a clear edge: a route or a capability whose data and callers are few. Start with a low-risk one to learn the process. A slice that shares a lot of data with others is expensive to move early, because while it lives in the new system and its neighbours in the old one, the data links across the boundary have to be kept consistent.

howItWorks.title: Prove parity before users see it
howItWorks.text: Build the slice in the new system, then run it in shadow mode: real requests go to both systems, the legacy answer is returned to the user, and the new answer is only compared (the new side must not commit writes or side effects such as charging a card, so it runs against a copy or in a dry-run mode). Every difference is either a bug in the new code or a quirk of the old one that someone depends on. A bug that fires on 1 in 1,000 requests is expected to show up once in about 1,000 shadowed requests, and catching it with 95 percent confidence takes about 3,000.

howItWorks.title: Ramp traffic in steps, with a way back
howItWorks.text: Route 1 percent of the slice's traffic to the new code, then 10, then 50, then all, watching error rates and business metrics at each step. If a monitor alerts, the router sends the traffic back to the legacy system, which is still there. The ramp limits how many users a bug reaches, but it only reveals bugs that are loud enough for the monitor to see at that share.

howItWorks.title: Finish: retire the old, delete the seam
howItWorks.text: When a slice has run at 100 percent for long enough, remove its legacy code and its data sync. When all slices are moved, remove the router rules and the legacy system. Give the migration an end date and track the slices left, because the temporary two-system state has a running cost that rises the longer it lasts.

pros: Real users reach the new system early, so value arrives and mistakes are found while they are small
Each slice is a small release that can be rolled back by changing a route
Shadow comparison finds differences from legacy behaviour before users do
The team can change its plan as it learns, instead of following a long-fixed rewrite
cons: Two systems run at once for months or years, with a router, a sync layer and double operations
Data shared across the boundary must be kept consistent while slices are split between old and new
Shadow runs and ramp-ups take engineering time and tooling that a big-bang plan does not budget for
The old system's quirks (the behaviour users rely on without anyone writing it down) have to be found and copied or consciously dropped
whenToUse: The legacy system is too important to stop and too large to rewrite and switch in one step
The system can be split into routes or capabilities that a router can send separately
You need the new system to prove itself against real traffic and real data, slice by slice
whenNotToUse: A small system that can be rewritten and replaced in a few weeks, where the router and sync layer cost more than they save
A system with no seam: one tangled transaction across everything, so no slice can run alone
When nobody will own the end: the migration will stall with both systems alive and the costs doubled
pitfalls: Routing without parity checks: a ramp alone costs 670 requests to bugs that a shadow run would have caught for 49, and a bug too quiet for the monitor stays silent
Moving each slice in one step, so bugs that would have been cheap at 1 percent hit 4,461 requests in this model, against 670 with a 1, 10, 50, 100 ramp (both without parity checks)
Slices so small (24 of them) that 12 data links cross the boundary at the worst moment and every route is a rule to maintain
Shadow runs too short to see rare bugs: a bug that fires once per 1,000 requests is missed by a replay of 500 about 6 times in 10
Retiring the old system's rollback early, so a late-found bug has to be fixed forward over several days
A migration with no end date: both systems stay live, and the temporary router and sync layer become permanent
Ignoring the data: the router moves requests, but the shared database or the data sync is usually the hardest part

roles.label: Users
roles.description: Send the traffic that the migration must keep serving.

roles.label: Router
roles.description: The proxy or gateway that decides, slice by slice, which system answers.

roles.label: Legacy system
roles.description: The system being replaced, kept as the source of truth and the way back.

roles.label: New system
roles.description: Takes over one slice at a time.

roles.label: Monitoring
roles.description: Compares answers and watches error rates to trigger a rollback.

quiz.question: A team ramps each migrated slice from 1 percent to 100 percent but never replays traffic to compare the new answers with the old. What is the main risk?
options: The ramp is too slow, so the migration never finishes.
The router becomes a single point of failure.
Bugs that are too quiet for the monitor stay silent, and louder ones still reach real users before they are noticed.
The legacy system will run out of capacity.
quiz.explanation: A ramp limits how many users a bug reaches, but users still see it, and only bugs that move an alerted metric are noticed. Shadow comparison finds differences before any user does, and also finds quiet ones.

quiz.question: Why is a big-bang rewrite risky compared with a strangler migration?
options: New code is always worse than old code.
Nothing reaches real users until the end, then all traffic switches at once, often with no practical way back.
quiz.explanation: The big-bang plan concentrates all the risk in one cutover that is hard or impossible to roll back, after a long period with no real-world feedback. Slice-by-slice migration spreads the risk into small steps that each have a way back.

quiz.question: A team cuts the migration into slices of one endpoint each, 24 in all. Which cost grows?
options: The number of routes to manage and data links that cross the old and new systems at the worst moment.
The amount of traffic exposed in a single step.
The time before the first user reaches the new system.
quiz.explanation: Smaller slices lower exposure and bring the first release earlier, but every slice is a route to maintain, and neighbouring slices that share data are more often split across the boundary, which needs sync code.
